**Role:** Technical Lead

::: {.project-hero-tags}
`CI/CD` `pytest` `Row-Level Security` `dbt` `GitLab CI`
:::

:::

## The Problem {.project-section-heading}

As the analytics platform grew to a family of production dashboard apps,
three structural risks grew with it: no automated gate stopped an
untested regression from merging, no consistent pattern existed for
scoping who can see what data, and a meaningful amount of business logic
lived scattered across application code instead of governed, testable
data models.


## The Approach {.project-section-heading}

### Test coverage, then a real CI gate

Rather than jump straight to a code-review process, I audited test
coverage app-by-app first — the reasoning being that reviewing code
nothing ever tests is "checking on sand." That survey found real gaps:
one app's security-admin pattern had zero access-control tests at all;
several others had only smoke-test-level coverage. I closed the highest-risk
gaps first, then stood up a pytest job in the CI pipeline so a merge with
failing tests is now visibly blocked rather than silently shipping.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 8
flowchart LR
    A[Audit Test Coverage<br>Per App] --> B[Close Highest-Risk<br>Gaps First]
    B --> C[CI Runs pytest<br>on Every Merge]
    C --> D[Regression Caught<br>Before It Ships]
```

### A reusable security pattern

Rather than let each dashboard invent its own row-level-security
implementation, I authored a portable pattern — piloted first in one app
— covering the admin UI, the scope-enforcement logic, and a documented
list of real bugs already hit during the pilot, so a future port
inherits the fixes instead of repeating the mistakes.

### Per-app deployments and a starter scaffold

In September 2026 I reworked the CI/CD pipeline so each app deploys on
its own: a change to one dashboard builds and ships only that dashboard,
and every app carries its own semantic version tag (`<app>/vX.Y.Z`)
instead of one repo-wide release number. The deploy runbook documents the
UAT-to-PROD path and the versioning rules. I also extracted a
`base-suite` scaffold — the trimmed common core the existing apps had
converged on, with a test job built into its CI snippet and two fleet-wide
defects (error-detail leakage on the deep health check, an unbounded
auth cache) fixed rather than copied forward — so the next app starts
from the settled shape instead of a copy of whichever app is nearest.

### A data-logic migration plan

I led an audit of business logic living in application code (joins,
aggregations, recoding) that belonged in governed dbt SQL models instead
— cataloging roughly 139 candidate items across every app on the
platform, then prioritizing and sequencing them so the highest-value,
lowest-risk items move first. Several of the highest-priority items have
already shipped, each verified against live production data before
cutover, not just tested in isolation.

### What Changed for the Business

- **Regressions get caught before they ship** — a merge with a failing
  test is now a visible, blocking signal instead of a silent risk
- **Security stops being reinvented per app** — one documented, tested
  pattern instead of five different ad-hoc implementations
- **A clear roadmap for data governance** — instead of "someday we should
  clean this up," a prioritized, sequenced plan the team can actually
  execute against

| Data Governance | dbt, PostgreSQL | Migration target for application-layer business logic |
